definition: Google Translate is a multilingual neural machine translation service developed by Google to translate text, documents and websites from one language into another.
details: It offers a website interface, a mobile app for Android and iOS, and an API that helps developers build browser extensions and software applications. As of September 2026, Google Translate supports 249 languages and language varieties at various levels. It served over 200 million people daily in May 2013, and over 500 million total users as of April 2016, with more than 100 billion words translated daily. Launched on April 28, 2006 as a statistical machine translation service, it originally used United Nations and European Parliament documents and transcripts to gather linguistic data. Rather than translating languages directly, it first translated text to English and then pivoted to the target language in most of the language combinations it posited in its grid, with a few exceptions including Catalan–Spanish. During a translation, it looked for patterns in millions of documents to help decide which words to choose and how to arrange them in the target language. In recent years, it has used a deep learning model to power its translations. Its accuracy, which has been criticized on several occasions, has been measured to vary greatly across languages. explainer.lead: Google Translate is Google's service for turning text, documents and websites from one language into another through its website, mobile apps and developer API. It makes translation available at very large scale, although its accuracy differs considerably across languages.

tiers.eli5: It is like a very well-read helper that has seen huge amounts of writing and suggests how to say something in another language. You give it a sentence, choose the language you want, and it writes a new version. It can be very handy, but it is not equally good at every language and can make mistakes.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers can call its API from browser extensions or other software, while the website and Android/iOS apps cover direct use. Typical settings are the source and target languages and the content to translate; as of September 2026, it supports 249 languages and language varieties at various levels. Test output for each language pair and add human review where mistakes matter, because accuracy varies greatly.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, it can be viewed as a learned mapping T(x, s, t) -> y, where x is source content, s and t are the source and target languages, and y is generated target-language content. It launched on April 28, 2006 as a statistical machine translation service using linguistic data gathered from United Nations and European Parliament documents and transcripts, often pivoting through English; recent versions use deep learning. Its measured accuracy varies greatly across languages, so one service-wide quality figure would not describe its limits.

explainer.example: You enter the Spanish sentence "¿Dónde está la estación?" and select English as the target language. Google Translate returns "Where is the station?"

explainer.intuition: Rather than relying only on hand-written bilingual rules, Google Translate learns from large collections of text how words and phrases tend to correspond. Its early system searched millions of documents for patterns; recent translations are powered by a deep learning model.
howItWorks: A user or application supplies text, a document or a website and chooses the source and target languages.
The request reaches the service through its website, Android or iOS app, or developer API.
The current deep learning model generates a translation; historically, the statistical system chose and arranged words using patterns found in millions of documents.
The translated result is returned in the interface or to the calling software.
explainer.whyItMatters: By April 2016, it had over 500 million total users and translated more than 100 billion words daily, showing the reach of automated translation. Its uneven accuracy also makes checking important when the result has real consequences.
misconceptions: It has not always been neural: it began as a statistical machine translation service in 2006.
The old English-pivot design should not be assumed to describe today's deep learning system.
Support for a language does not imply the same accuracy as in every other language.
